headline: OpenAI and Anthropic told a committee of British MPs that voluntary safety pledges are no longer enough and that binding rules are needed, while Google DeepMind and Meta would not back new laws.
score_reason: Pool score kept: two leading AI labs publicly asked a parliament for binding rules and UK officials admitted the regime is voluntary, reported first-hand by WIRED, but it is testimony, not legislation.
importance_line: People in Britain and elsewhere could get binding AI safety rules sooner if governments follow the two labs' call, which matters to regulators, to the UK's AI Security Institute and to the other AI companies, but this was testimony to MPs, not legislation, and Google DeepMind and Meta did not back it.
summary: WIRED reports that Liam Booth-Smith, Anthropic's head of Europe, told the UK parliament's Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee on Tuesday 13 Oct 2026 that "the rules should be binding", and that Tom Duff Gordon, an OpenAI vice president, backed a statutory framework with some mandatory elements, starting with incident reporting, while representatives of Google DeepMind and Meta would not back new legislation. The UK's AI Security Institute, which tests frontier models before release, told the same session that it relies on companies handing models over and cannot stop a release, and Cat Little, the Cabinet Office's top civil servant, agreed the system is voluntary "at the moment".
notes: Full WIRED text read (pre-fetched file). Only WIRED found covering the session, so status REPORTED. The names of the Google DeepMind and Meta representatives are left out of the summary because WIRED gives no job titles. Related: our 6 Oct 2026 edition carried the Australian inquiry where the same two labs said they would welcome breach-reporting laws.
